title: Ninety Days and Thirteen Thousand Bricks
subtitle: Two companies near the edge of ruin had far too many things to fix. Both began, not with what to add, but with what to stop, and with the one thing the rest depended on.
intention: you'll see why a priority question needs an order and a reason for it, sort what is urgent from what is only loud, and say what you are leaving out, as well as what comes first.
warmup: Without looking back: what are the four questions of the choosing lens from the last lesson, and what does it mean to ‘name the price’ of a pick?
What was loud in your work last week, and what was actually important? Were they the same thing?
When you have too much to do, what is the first thing you do: make a list, ask someone, or start with whatever is nearest?

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the context
vocab.intro: Read the sentence, guess the meaning of the word in bold, then reveal.

items.sent: In an emergency ward, nurses use triage: the patients in the greatest danger are treated first, whatever order they arrived in.
items.meaning: triage — sorting problems or people by urgency, so that the most serious are dealt with first. Also used for any crowded to-do list.

items.sent: The slow approval step was the bottleneck: every other part of the project had to wait for it.
items.meaning: bottleneck — a point where progress is held up, limiting how fast everything else can move.

items.sent: The toy maker tried to diversify into clothes, theme parks and video games all at once, and lost sight of what it did best.
items.meaning: diversify — to expand into a range of different products, markets or activities. Noun: diversification.

items.sent: After two quiet years, the finance director decided that cash was the only thing that mattered for now and everything else could wait: survival first.
items.meaning: survival first — putting the continued existence of the organisation ahead of growth or any other goal, in a crisis.

vocab.heading: B · Which term means…?
vocab.intro: Three terms: the vital few · a quick win · scope creep. Say the right one, then reveal.

items.sent: Which term means the gradual growth of a project beyond its original aims, usually without a decision to expand it?
items.meaning: scope creep — The brief began as one report and, through scope creep, became a whole programme.

items.sent: Which term means the small number of causes or items that produce most of the results?
items.meaning: the vital few — A handful of faults caused most of the complaints; those were the vital few.

items.sent: Which term means an easy success achieved quickly, often used to build confidence in a plan?
items.meaning: a quick win — Fixing the broken form was a quick win that convinced the sceptics.

vocab.heading: C · Which word completes all three phrases?
vocab.intro: One missing word fits every phrase in the group. Say it, then reveal.

items.sent: a top ___  ·  a clear ___  ·  a shifting ___
items.meaning: priority — something that is more important than other things and needs attention first. Plural: priorities.

items.sent: clear the ___  ·  a growing ___  ·  a ___ of unanswered emails
items.meaning: backlog — a pile of work that should already have been done.

items.sent: draw the ___  ·  cross the ___  ·  a fine ___
items.meaning: line — draw the line means to set a limit on what you will accept or do.

vocab_use: What is the bottleneck in a process you know well? What would change if it were removed?
Tell me about a time something that started small became scope creep. When should someone have drawn the line?
If you had to triage your own week right now, what would be your top priority, and what would you drop?

story.heading: Part 1 — Ninety days from empty
paras: In 1985, Apple’s co-founder Steve Jobs lost a boardroom battle and left the company he had started. Through the early 1990s the company that remained was profitable for a while, then steadily less so. Computers running Microsoft Windows took more and more of the market. Apple responded by making more: many versions of the Macintosh with confusing model numbers, printers, early digital cameras, a handheld organiser called the Newton, even a games console. It also began licensing its operating system to other makers, whose cheaper copies mainly took sales from Apple itself.

By mid-1997 Apple was losing money fast, roughly a billion dollars that financial year. The share price had collapsed, respected commentators were suggesting it should be sold or closed, and the chief executive was removed in July. Jobs, who had returned when Apple bought his later company NeXT, later said that the company had been within about ninety days of running out of money. He agreed to lead it on a temporary basis.

He began with cuts. In August 1997 he announced a deal that shocked a conference audience: Microsoft would invest 150 million dollars in non-voting Apple shares and commit to making its Office software for the Mac for at least five years. He ended the licensing programme. And he reviewed the product line, found dozens of products and variations, and reduced the future to a grid of four boxes: computers for consumers and for professionals, each as a desktop and a portable. Most other products and projects were stopped, including the Newton and the printers. In 1998 the new operations chief, Tim Cook, cut inventory from months of stock to days. In May 1998 the iMac arrived, and Apple was profitable again for the year.
checks: What did Apple do in response to losing market share in the early 1990s?
What did Jobs say about the company’s finances in 1997?
What were the first things he stopped, and what grid did he keep?
answers: It made more: many confusing versions of the Mac, printers, cameras, a handheld organiser and even a games console, and it licensed its operating system to other makers whose cheaper machines took its own sales.
That the company had been within about ninety days of running out of money.

He ended the licensing programme and stopped most products and projects, including the Newton and the printers. He kept a grid of four boxes: consumer and professional computers, each as a desktop and a portable.
story.discuss: Adding products is often the first response to losing ground. When has your organisation, or one you know, tried to grow its way out of a problem that was really about focus?

story.heading: Part 2 — Thirteen thousand bricks
paras: By 2003 the Lego Group, family-owned since 1932, was losing money at a rate that threatened its existence. Sales had fallen sharply, debt had climbed towards the billion-dollar mark, and the owners were advised that they might have to sell. The strange part was how it had happened. Lego had not been lazy; it had been frantic. Convinced that children were abandoning physical toys for screens, the company had diversified in every direction at once: theme parks, clothing, watches, video games, television tie-ins, its own shops.

The problem ran down to the plastic. Designers, freed from commercial discipline, had multiplied the number of distinct brick shapes and colours to around thirteen thousand, many used once, each requiring its own steel mould. Nobody could say with confidence which products made money.

In 2004 the owner handed the company to Jørgen Vig Knudstorp, a thirty-five-year-old former consultant, the first chief executive from outside the family. His opening message was deliberately unheroic: there would be no inspiring vision for a while. Survival first. Cash mattered more than growth. The theme parks were sold, the clothing and other sidelines were licensed out or closed, and the number of brick elements was roughly halved, to six or seven thousand. Every new mould and colour now needed a business case. The company turned back to its core play themes. Profitability returned within two years, and by the mid-2010s Lego had overtaken Mattel to become one of the largest toy companies in the world.
checks: Why does the case say Lego was ‘frantic’ and not ‘lazy’?
What did the new chief executive’s opening message say, and why was it unusual?
What were three of the things stopped or reduced?
answers: Because it had reacted to a perceived threat by diversifying in every direction at once, into parks, clothes, watches, games and more, and had multiplied its brick shapes, rather than doing too little.
That there would be no inspiring vision for a while: survival and cash came first. It was unusual because new leaders normally promise a big idea.
Any three: the theme parks were sold; clothing and other sidelines were licensed out or closed; the number of brick elements was roughly halved; every new mould or colour needed a business case.
story.discuss: Lego’s new leader refused to offer a vision. What does a leader gain, and what do they risk, by saying ‘survival first’?

story.heading: Part 3 — The order of work, and the order of leaving out
paras: Both companies faced the same question in a different form: what do we do first? And both answered it in the same unusual way. They did not begin with what to build. They began with what to stop.

Use the lens. What is urgent, and what is only loud? Urgent: the cash running out, ninety days away at Apple and an annual loss in the hundreds of millions at Lego. Loud: a games console, a clothing line, a thousand model numbers. Which few matter most? Apple’s four boxes, and Lego’s core play themes. What depends on what? At Apple, the Microsoft agreement made the platform safe for business customers, and the software deal made everything else possible. At Lego, nothing could grow until the cost of producing thousands of one-use pieces was brought under control.

The answers were not only about what came first. Most of the work was about what to leave, and about saying so. Both leaders closed whole areas of activity, and both kept their messages simple. The honest question the lens leaves open is whether ‘focus’ is a permanent principle, or only a rule for emergencies. A company that has recovered must still decide what to start again.
checks: What was urgent at each company, and what was merely loud?
What did the Microsoft agreement make possible at Apple?
What question does the lens leave open?
answers: Urgent: the lack of cash (ninety days at Apple; large annual losses at Lego). Loud: the many products and projects, such as the games console, clothing lines and model numbers.
It reassured business customers and software makers that essential software would stay on the Mac, which made the rest of the recovery plan possible.
Whether focus is a permanent principle or only a rule for emergencies, and what a recovered company should start again.
story.discuss: When you say ‘not now’ to something, how do you make sure the other person hears a reason, and not a rejection?

tool_tab.lead: A “What first…?” question asks for an order. It is common when there is too much to do and not enough people, time or money. The lens helps you sort what is urgent from what is only loud, find the few things that matter most, and see which tasks unlock the rest. It is a thinking aid: it gets you to an order you can defend, not to the one perfect order.

outcomes.d: important, but|not yet urgent:|give it a date
someone else can|do it as well|as you can
say so, and|give a reason:|“not now”

how: What is urgent, and what is only loud? Urgent means a cost is arriving soon. Loud means someone is shouting. They are not the same.
Which few matter most? Look for the vital few: the one or two causes that produce most of the trouble or most of the value.
What depends on what? Some tasks unblock all the others. Do those first, even if they are not the most visible.
Say the order, and say what you are leaving. I would start with… because… The rest can wait, and here is what I would not do.

sort.intro: Each situation describes one item on a long list. Where does the lens put it? Choose, then check.

items.text: A payment error is stopping customers from completing orders today. Every other fix depends on it.
items.why: it is urgent (orders are failing now) and it blocks everything else.

items.text: A colleague asks you to redesign the office intranet. It matters to him, nobody else would notice, and the web team can do it well.
items.why: someone else can do it as well as you can, so your time is better spent elsewhere.

items.text: A training plan will improve everyone’s skills over the next year. Nothing breaks if it waits a week, but it never happens unless a date is set.
items.why: it is important but not urgent, so it needs a date and not a ‘when I have time’.

items.text: A monthly report has become a ritual: nobody reads it, no decision depends on it, and it takes a day to produce.
items.why: it produces no value; stopping it, and saying so, frees a day each month.

items.text: A client has said they will leave unless a promised report arrives by Friday.
items.why: a real cost is arriving on a fixed date and the client has said so.

items.text: The budget review for next quarter is important, but it is not due until next month.
items.why: it is important and not yet urgent, so schedule it before it becomes urgent.

items.text: A new colleague could handle the weekly data entry just as well as you, and it takes you three hours every week.
items.why: the task does not need you, and handing it on frees time for work only you can do.

breaks: Everything really is urgent. Sometimes it is. Then the lens helps you say what you can still delay by a day, and what would cost most if it slipped.

The ranking itself is disputed. Two people may rank the same list differently because they care about different things. Say your criterion out loud so the argument is about that and not about the list.
Urgent is a feeling. A loud request can feel urgent. Ask: what exactly happens, and when, if this waits?
discuss: What is the one thing in your work that is always urgent and almost never important? What would happen if it were left?
How do you tell a colleague that their request comes last, and keep their trust?

grammar.name: Sequencing and focus
grammar.lead: A priority answer is mostly about order. This language says what comes first, what depends on it, and what matters most, in a way that sounds composed.
notes: Ordering words: first and foremost · to begin with · once · until · only then · in the meantime · lastly. Once the payments work, we can look at the login delay. Only then should we think about redesign.

Negative inversion (for emphasis): after only when, only after, not until, hardly, never, the auxiliary comes before the subject. Only when the payments work can we test the other fixes. Not until the cash was secure did the company start to invest. Hardly had one fix been finished when another problem appeared.
Focus with a cleft: What matters most is the payment error. It is the cash that needs fixing first. The cleft puts the important part in the stressed position.

exercises.heading: Emphasis and inversion
exercises.intro: Write one word, or the verb form given, in each gap.
items: 1. ___ when the payments work can we test the other fixes.
2. Not until the cash was secure did the company ___ (start) to invest again.
3. What matters most ___ the payment error, not the typos.
4. Hardly had the team finished one fix ___ another problem appeared.
answers: 2. start — base form after did in the inverted clause
4. when — Hardly… when… for two events in quick succession

exercises.heading: Put it in order
exercises.intro: Use each expression from the box once: first and foremost · until · only then · once.
items: 1. ___, we need the payment errors fixed; they are costing us orders.
2. We will not begin the redesign ___ every fix has been tested.
3. ___ the payments work, we can look at the login delay.
4. The cash must be secure. ___ should the company think about new products.
answers: 1. First and foremost — the first and most important thing
2. until — not… until marks the point at which it can begin
3. Once — introduces a condition that must be completed first
4. Only then — the next step is allowed only after the previous one

grammar.closing: Now say a priority order for a real list of tasks, out loud: use first and foremost and one of only when…can we… or not until…did…, and say what you are leaving out.

speak.intro: Say the order, say the reason, and say what you are leaving. Choose a task, start the timer, and talk.
speak.useful: “First and foremost…” · “The urgent thing is… the important thing is…” · “Only when… can we…” · “What depends on that is…” · “I’d leave… for now, because…” · “Not now, and here is why.”

tasks.label: Task 1 — Where do we start?
paras: Choose one: You have six problems and one week. A team has five projects and two people. You run a small shop with too much stock and too few customers. Name three of the items, say which comes first and why, and say one thing you would leave.

tasks.label: Task 2 — Urgent or loud?
paras: Describe something that felt urgent and was only loud, or something quiet that turned out to be urgent. Say how you could tell, and what you would do differently now.

tasks.label: Task 3 — Not now
paras: Someone asks you to take on a new task. Say no in under thirty seconds: give the reason, say what you are protecting, and offer a date when you could look at it.

final: Apple and Lego both began by stopping things. What is the difference between focus and simply doing less?
Is it ever right to put the quiet, important task behind the loud, urgent one? When, and who decides?
‘Survival first’ means putting growth to one side. How long can a company say that before it becomes an excuse?
From memory: explain the three questions of the lens in four sentences, using urgent, the vital few, bottleneck and only then.
